title: Why Andy Burnham must back an International Panel on Inequality
gist: Stiglitz and LSE president Larry Kramer urge new UK prime minister Andy Burnham to champion an International Panel on Inequality — an IPCC-style body of some 40 experts being designed by South Africa, Brazil, Norway and Spain after a G20 proposal — arguing the most unequal countries are seven times more likely to suffer democratic erosion and that as little as 1 per cent of wealth generated since 2000 has reached the poorest half of humanity.

insights.claim: The most unequal countries are now seven times more likely to experience democratic erosion, making inequality a direct driver of political instability rather than merely a social concern.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A quantified link between distributional outcomes and regime stability — directly relevant to sovereign political-risk models.
insights.quote: the most unequal countries are now seven times more likely to experience democratic erosion
insights.locator: The extremes of inequality we see today

insights.claim: Only a small fraction of all wealth generated since 2000 — by some estimates as little as 1 per cent — has reached the poorest half of humanity, while similar estimates put more than 40 per cent with the richest 1 per cent worldwide.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: The headline distributional number that will anchor the political case for wealth taxation and global redistribution mechanisms.
insights.locator: Recent data on growing international wealth inequality is striking.

insights.claim: Inequality is framed as the cumulative result of decades of government choices and therefore reversible — a policy choice rather than a structural inevitability.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: This framing is the precondition for interventionist policy; if it wins, expect more aggressive redistribution and industrial policy.
insights.quote: But inequality is a policy choice, and its extremes can be reversed.

insights.claim: In left-behind communities, research identifies a recognisable symptom cluster: deep mistrust of politics, blaming immigrant communities for societal problems, and a distinct lack of belief that society can work for normal people.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A diagnostic linking regional economic divergence to anti-immigration politics — the mechanism behind populist vote share in deindustrialised regions.
insights.locator: In communities that have been ignored

insights.claim: An International Panel on Inequality was proposed at last year's G20 and would function like the IPCC — the world's scientific authority on inequality, assembling experts across disciplines to build a shared scientific consensus on its drivers and consequences.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: Institutionalising an evidence consensus is how climate policy became mandatory; the same playbook applied to inequality would reshape tax and transfer debates.
insights.locator: at last year’s G20, a proposal designed to meet the scale

insights.claim: The IPI's details are being developed by the governments of South Africa, Brazil, Norway and Spain working with the expert group that made the G20 proposal, and it would see some 40 leading inequality experts operate with full academic freedom.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: Names the specific sponsor states and scale — a concrete institution-building process to monitor into the UN General Assembly.
insights.locator: The details of the IPI are now in the process of being developed

insights.claim: The proposal has garnered support from academics and governments worldwide and from the UN secretary-general, and the authors argue Burnham must champion it ahead of the UN General Assembly this September.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A dated diplomatic catalyst: UK endorsement at UNGA would materially raise the IPI's odds of being established.
insights.locator: The idea has now garnered enormous support

insights.claim: The UK is gearing up to take over the G20, giving it agenda-setting power the authors want used to export “Burnhamism” as a global economic model.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: UK G20 presidency is the institutional window for any British-led inequality agenda — watch the agenda-setting announcements.
insights.quote: As the UK gears up to take over the G20, we urge him to go one step further and bring Burnhamism, his vision for a new economic model, to the world stage.
insights.locator: In his resounding victory in the Makerfield byelection

themes.theme: Burnhamism and the end of growth-at-all-costs

insights.claim: In his first remarks as UK leader, Merseyside-born Andy Burnham promised a new political model and explicitly criticised the “wrong turns” of privatisation and nationwide deindustrialisation under the neoliberalism that has gripped Britain since the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A sitting UK prime minister repudiating privatisation is a regime change for UK utilities, rail and public-service contracting risk.
insights.locator: In his first remarks as the UK’s new leader

insights.claim: Burnham's organising principle is the “Makerfield Test” — the standard that “if it does not work for Makerfield—it does not work” — through which he pledges to give citizens more control over their economy.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A stated decision rule for UK policy: expect proposals to be screened for distributional effect on deprived towns, not aggregate GDP.
insights.quote: if it does not work for Makerfield—it does not work
insights.locator: In his resounding victory in the Makerfield byelection

insights.claim: Burnham appears to be rejecting the “growth at all costs” narrative that has dominated UK economic discourse, on the view that the quality and direction of growth matters more than the headline rate.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: If the UK downgrades headline GDP as the policy objective, expect distributional conditions attached to investment, procurement and planning decisions.
insights.locator: As a solution, Burnham appears to be lightly rejecting

insights.claim: The stated causal chain is that booming private wealth alongside shrinking public wealth reinforced inequalities in health, education, housing and social protection across the country.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: Public-balance-sheet restoration is the implied policy response — relevant to UK public investment and borrowing assumptions.
insights.locator: He knows that as private wealth has boomed

insights.claim: Rumours are swirling that Burnham will course-correct on the UK's recent aid-budget cuts, restoring efforts to tackle global poverty.
insights.speaker: Larry Kramer, Joseph E. Stiglitz
insights.so_what: A reversal of UK ODA cuts would be a reweighting of the development-finance landscape; treat as speculative until confirmed.
insights.locator: While the UK has reduced its aid budget in recent years
